newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland, Jews lay groundwork for Auschwitz plan.
newsitem.headline: Poland, Jews lay groundwork for Auschwitz plan.

text.p: Poland and international Jewish organisations on Wednesday agreed ground rules for a scheme to better preserve the former Auschwitz-Birkenau death camps while helping the adjacent Polish town of Oswiecim to develop.

A central aim is to avoid further rows between Poles and Jews over the south Poland camp complex where German invaders in World War Two murdered up to 1.5 million people -- the vast majority Jews but also tens of thousands of Poles.

"We are trying to lay the groundwork for the physical, geographical and spiritual integrity of this unique site in a way that will preserve it for generations and avoid the periodic controversies which end up dividing us all," American Jewish Committee Executive Director David Harris said.

Polish government officials, Jewish groups led by U.S. Holocaust Memorial Council Chairman Miles Lerman, the board of the Auschwitz museum and the mayor of Oswiecim town signed a declaration on principles for implementing a long-term scheme for the area, initiated by Poland last year.
The twin camps of Auschwitz-Birkenau have repeatedly been at the centre of controversy.

Jewish groups, stressing that Birkenau is the world's largest Jewish graveyard, have objected to Polish Catholics who opened a convent by Auschwitz -- now gone -- and put up crosses and Jewish symbols which remain standing in Birkenau itself.
Residents of Oswiecim bridled at calls for strict limits on urban development to preserve protected zones around the camps which were declared by UNESCO in 1979 but patchily enforced.
Last year plans by a developer to open a shopping centre right near the current main gate of the Auschwitz museum aroused Jewish protests that it was crassly inappropriate.

Polish authorities and President Aleksander Kwasniewski, bent on improving ties with the Jewish diaspora and Israel, halted the shop and unveiled a costly, long-term programme for improving conservation while helping the run-down town.
The document signed on Wednesday was the result of three days of consultations in Warsaw and Oswiecim with Jewish groups who have offered their own ideas and are raising funds.

The document recognised some issues remain unresolved, notably the presence of crosses and other symbols, which anger many Jews. It calls for a suitable solution respectful of the sensitivities of all parties to be found as soon as possible.

Lerman, who heads the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington, said the plan aimed to ensure that Auschwitz was linked as a single entity with the less well-preserved Birkenau. This could involve creating a new, common entrance complex between the two camps which are three km (two miles) apart.
Lerman said the plan would ensure that the protected zone was fully implemented, although this would be done flexibly.
It would help Oswiecim benefit by catering for increasing numbers of visitors who now travel from nearby Krakow but could stay in the town itself and bring business to it.
The common entrance to both sites will be far enough away from each to allow shops, hotels and restaurants to be provided without offence, architects advising the Jewish groups said.
Apart from funds being provided by the Polish government, the Jewish organisations have been gathering pledges for conservation of the former camp sites themselves.
Lerman told reporters they had a target figure of $42 million and had so far raised $23 million in commitments from European governments and other donors.
